query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Localized surface compositional segregation in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles triggers an initial liquid-like layer above a critical temperature, causing the premelting front to initiate at the particle periphery and propagate inward, thereby governing both the onset and progression of the phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles of uniform size distribution.
generation.intervention: Time-resolved environmental TEM heating with controlled ramp rates (1–10 K/s) under inert or low-pressure conditions, allowing in situ observation of morphological and diffraction changes.
generation.conditions: Temperatures spanning from below to above the anticipated melting range (e.g., 600–1300 K), with continuous electron beam imaging for compositional and structural analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface-segregated layers forming incipient liquids at elevated temperature.
generation.mechanism: The segregation of species with lower melting points to the nanoparticle surface increases local atomic mobility, enabling a transient liquid-like phase at the perimeter that nucleates and spreads inward, culminating in full melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Early-onset melting at the nanoparticle surface, verified by high-resolution imaging and diffraction signatures of liquid shells forming at lower temperatures than would be expected if melting were homogeneously nucleated in the bulk.
generation.baseline: Under identical heating conditions, single-element nanoparticles of similar size lacking multi-element segregation show a narrower transition region and a higher, more uniform melting temperature.
generation.boundary: For larger (>20 nm) FeNiCrCoCu particles or significantly altered heating environments (e.g., high oxygen partial pressure), the sequence and temperature of melting onset may deviate from the proposed surface-driven mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range of surface premelting may vary with particle size, composition, and local thermodynamic fluctuations, so predictions of the exact melting point have limited precision.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel TEM heating experiments on FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with systematically altered surface compositions (e.g., surface passivation to suppress segregation) under identical heating rates and environments. Track real-time structural evolution via electron diffraction and composition via EDS/EELS mapping.
measurements: Onset temperature of the first liquid-like signatures at the particle surface.
Spatial progression of molten regions observed in real time.
Comparative meltdown temperatures and melting sequences between unmodified and surface-passivated nanoparticles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles do not exhibit surface-initiated melting at reduced temperatures, or if the progression to a fully molten state does not correlate with an incipient liquid-like surface layer, then the proposed surface-segregation-driven mechanism is falsified.

Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. However, the common extreme high temperature related approaches such as arc melting and laser cladding are not suitable for supporting HEA-NPs due to the rapid growth and aggregation of nanoparticles. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM. decision.trend: Initial work (PMC7733500, 2020) highlighted how metallic nanoparticles form and stabilize on carbon supports under high-temperature processing conditions, demonstrating that phase transitions can be directly observed via in situ methods. Later (PMC10056590, 2023), researchers broadened their focus to the CrMnFeCoNiCu system, showing that compositional adjustments and controlled processing temperatures influence microstructure evolution and phase stability. Most recently, efforts to synthesize CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles via laser solid-phase processes (PMC11427457, 2024) underscored how high-rate heating and rapid solidification produce unique core–shell structures but have yet to clarify precisely how premelting and melting transitions initiate and progress in FeNiCrCoCu systems under sustained high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, the exact mechanism governing the onset and progression of phase transitions in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles remains uncertain. Specifically, it is unclear how nanoscale compositional fluctuations, surface-segregation phenomena, and potential liquid-like surface layers interact to trigger premelting and drive the transition to a fully molten state, preventing a reliable mapping of operational temperature limits for high-temperature synthesis.
decision.lever: Time-resolved environmental TEM heating experiments on size-selected FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles to monitor real-time morphological changes, chemical redistribution, and diffraction signatures of partial and full melting. The key parameters include a controlled ramp rate (e.g., 1–10 K/s) and variable atmosphere to discern the roles of surface segregation versus bulk diffusion in nuclear vs. surface-driven melting pathways.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the open question of how compositional gradients and surface effects precipitate melting in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles during high-temperature exposure. Building on the in situ insights from prior studies (PMC7733500) and the composition–structure relationships identified in FeNiCrCoCu-based alloys (PMC10056590) and CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles (PMC11427457), such experiments will elucidate the mechanistic origin of premelting phenomena and allow precise mapping of the temperature ranges for stable nanoparticle operation.
